questions.prompt: A fleet of parking meters writes one record each time a car leaves, all day, to a file that a nightly job reads. Which format suits that file best?
options: One JSON document holding an array of all the day's records
A Parquet file rewritten after every record
JSON Lines, one record per line, with its schema written down
A spreadsheet workbook saved after every record
questions.explanation: JSON Lines appends one complete record per line, so a writer adds a line and a reader streams them; the written schema covers what the text format cannot carry.
misconceptions: Treats a JSON array as appendable: the closing bracket means every append rewrites the file
Treats columnar as always best: Parquet files are written whole, not appended one record at a time
Treats a workbook as a log: rewriting a whole workbook per record is slow and fragile

questions.prompt: An analyst sums one column of a 40-column table of 50 million rows. Why does the Parquet copy answer faster than the CSV copy?
options: Parquet keeps the rows sorted, so the sum stops early
Parquet reads only that column's chunks, already typed
Parquet files hold fewer rows than the CSV
Parquet keeps the whole table in memory between queries
questions.explanation: Columns are stored together with their types, so the reader fetches one column's chunks and skips parsing text; a CSV must be read and parsed line by line.
misconceptions: Confuses statistics with sorting: a sum needs every value whatever the order
Assumes compression drops rows: the same data has the same rows in both files
Confuses a file format with a cache: a file on disk keeps nothing in memory

questions.prompt: One read of a CSV took 0.4 seconds and one read of the same data as Parquet took 0.6 seconds on a colleague's laptop. That is enough evidence to state that CSV reads faster than Parquet for this data.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: One timing on one machine moves with the cache and the run; compare medians of several reads on one machine, and trust sizes and type fidelity more than seconds.
misconceptions: Treats a single timing as a property of the format

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy writes dispensing records as Parquet. Most queries ask for one month, sometimes one ward. Which partition column fits?
options: The prescription number
The patient's record code
The dispensing month
The exact time of dispensing, to the second
questions.explanation: A partition column should match the common filter and have tens to hundreds of values; one folder per month lets a query open only its month.
misconceptions: Picks a unique key: one folder per prescription writes millions of tiny files
Picks an identifier people rarely filter on, and one with too many values
Picks the finest grain possible: almost every row gets its own folder

questions.prompt: A training centre's attendance export opens in pandas, the first column is visibly named trainee_code, yet df["trainee_code"] raises a KeyError. What is the likely cause?
options: A UTF-8 byte order mark glued to the first column name
The file uses semicolons instead of commas
The trainee codes have leading zeros
The file was saved with Windows line endings
questions.explanation: Read as plain UTF-8, the mark becomes an invisible character at the start of the first column name; utf-8-sig removes it.
misconceptions: Expects a wrong delimiter to rename one column: it would put every column into one
Confuses a value problem with a name problem: zeros change values, not column names
Expects line endings to change the header: pandas handles CRLF line endings

questions.prompt: Decoding a file as Windows-1256 can succeed without any error even when the file is really UTF-8.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Windows-1256 maps every byte to a character, so it never fails; it returns the wrong letters, which is why a known word must confirm the encoding.
misconceptions: Assumes a wrong encoding always raises an error

questions.prompt: The first bytes of a supplier's price list read ff fe 70 00 72 00 69 00. What is it?
options: A UTF-8 file with a byte order mark
A Windows-1256 file
A file that was double-encoded
UTF-16 text, little-endian
questions.explanation: ff fe is the UTF-16 little-endian mark, and a zero byte after each ASCII letter is how UTF-16 stores them.
misconceptions: Mixes up the marks: the UTF-8 mark is ef bb bf
Expects a single-byte code page to contain zero bytes: its letters are one byte each
Confuses two faults: double encoding is valid UTF-8 with wrong letters, not zero bytes

questions.prompt: A border-crossing camera logs times without offsets. Compared with a UTC reference, it is 60 minutes ahead in winter and 120 minutes ahead in summer. What is the right repair?
options: Subtract 90 minutes from every time
Read the times in the camera's zone, then convert to UTC
Subtract 60 minutes, the winter gap, from every time
Drop the summer months as unreliable
questions.explanation: A gap that changes with the date is a zone with daylight saving; only that zone's rules give each time its own offset.
misconceptions: Averages two offsets: every time ends up wrong by 30 minutes
Treats a changing gap as fixed: summer times stay an hour off
Throws data away instead of reading it right

questions.prompt: In a zone that leaves daylight saving in autumn, a bare local time inside the repeated hour can be placed in UTC from the time alone.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The repeated hour happens twice with two offsets; another clue, such as the order of events, is needed to choose the pass.
misconceptions: Assumes every local time names one instant

questions.prompt: A client of a weather-station API gets 401 Unauthorized on its first request. What should it do?
options: Retry with exponential backoff, up to six times
Wait one minute and try again
Stop and report it: the credentials are wrong or missing
Switch to the offset endpoint
questions.explanation: A 401 says the request itself is not allowed; repeating it adds load and can lock the token, so the client stops and reports.
misconceptions: Retries every error: backoff is for temporary failures such as 503
Treats an authorisation failure as a rate limit
Thinks a different endpoint bypasses authentication

questions.prompt: A city transit API answers 429 Too Many Requests with the header Retry-After: 30. What does a well-behaved client do next?
options: Waits 30 seconds, then sends the same request again
Sends the request again at once from a second token
Gives up on the pull and reports the API as down
Waits one second and doubles the page size
questions.explanation: The server has said how long to wait; honouring Retry-After is both polite and the fastest way back to a 200.
misconceptions: Evades the limit instead of respecting it, which breaks most APIs' terms
Treats a rate limit as an outage: the API is up and has said when to return
Ignores the header and asks for more per request, which may be limited too

questions.prompt: A client pages a news-alerts API by offset, newest first, 100 per page. During the pull, 15 new alerts are published. What happens?
options: Nothing changes: offsets are fixed when the pull starts
The client gets 15 alerts twice and never sees the 15 new ones
The client sees the 15 new alerts on its next page
The API returns an error and the pull restarts
questions.explanation: New items at the top shift every later item down, so the next offset repeats 15 already seen; a cursor names the last item seen and does not shift.
misconceptions: Assumes an offset is a snapshot: it is a position in a list that keeps changing
Expects new items to appear further down: newest first puts them before the current offset
Expects the API to detect the change: offset paging fails silently

questions.prompt: If a pull stops after writing a page's records but before saving its checkpoint, a rerun that skips ids already kept loads every record exactly once.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The rerun fetches that page again, and keying the write by id makes the second write change nothing: an idempotent load.
misconceptions: Assumes a page fetched twice must produce duplicates whatever the write does

questions.prompt: A colleague's notebook pulling from a ticketing API has the token typed into a cell. What is the safest change?
options: Put the token in a comment so it does not run
Split the token into two strings joined at run time
Clear the notebook's outputs before sharing it
Read it from an environment variable or an ignored .env file
questions.explanation: A token in code travels with every copy, history and output of the notebook; reading it from the environment keeps it out of all of them.
misconceptions: Thinks a comment hides it: the text is still in the file and its history
Thinks obfuscation is protection: anyone can join the two strings
Clears only outputs: the token stays in the cell's source

questions.prompt: Each order from a bakery's API holds a customer object and a list of items. How should it be flattened for analysis?
options: One wide table with columns item_1, item_2, item_3 and so on
An orders table and an items table that carries the order id
One table per customer
Keep each order's item list as a JSON string in one column
questions.explanation: Things that occur once per order become columns of the orders table; the list becomes its own table at the item grain, joined back by the order id.
misconceptions: Fixes the number of items in advance: a longer order breaks the table
Confuses grouping with flattening: tables are made per grain, not per value
Leaves the nesting in place: the items cannot be typed, filtered or summed

questions.prompt: After writing a partitioned Parquet dataset, how do you prove the files have the declared schema?
options: Print the first rows and look at them
Count the rows in each partition
Read the schema of a written file and compare it with the declared one
Check that the folder names start with the partition column
questions.explanation: The file's own schema is what readers will get: compare names, types, time zone and nullability with the declaration, leaving out the partition column that lives in the path.
misconceptions: Trusts printed values: a float and a decimal, or two time zones, can print alike
Checks completeness, not types
Checks the layout, not the content of the files

questions.prompt: In a hive-partitioned dataset, the partition column is stored inside every Parquet file as well as in the folder names.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The value lives in the folder name (day=2026-10-21); readers add it back as a column when they read the dataset.
misconceptions: Assumes every column of the table is in every file

questions.prompt: Every record of today's batch from a lab-results supplier has result_value renamed to value. What should the load do?
options: Reject the batch and report the changed field to the supplier
Quarantine all records one by one
Rename the field silently and load the batch
Load the batch with result_value left empty
questions.explanation: When every record breaks the same way, the interface changed: rejecting once names the cause, and the supplier fixes it at the source.
misconceptions: Hides one cause behind hundreds of row reports
Repairs a contract break without the owner knowing, so the next change goes unnoticed
Loads data that is known to be incomplete

questions.prompt: A load quarantines 6 rows of a 400-row batch from a school's attendance system. Who should act on them, and how?
options: The loader's author fixes the rows and loads them the same day
Nobody: quarantined rows are deleted after a week
The school's data owner corrects them at the source and resends; someone else reviews the release
The analyst who reads the tables fills in the gaps by hand
questions.explanation: Quarantine exists so owners see what failed; the owner corrects the source, and keeping release apart from the loader's author keeps the check honest.
misconceptions: Lets the person who wrote the checks also override them: no separation of duties
Treats quarantine as deletion: the owner never learns what failed
Patches the output instead of the source, so the fault returns next batch

questions.prompt: To show that a set of validation checks works, it must catch every seeded defect and also let a clean batch pass.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Catching defects alone is not enough: checks that reject everything would also catch them; the clean batch passing shows they reject only what is wrong.
misconceptions: Counts catching defects as enough, without a clean batch that must pass

questions.prompt: Which rule needs the whole batch, not one record at a time?
options: Every reading has a number for its value
Every time carries a UTC offset
No order id appears twice in the batch
The status is one of three allowed words
questions.explanation: Uniqueness compares rows with each other, so it runs on the table; types, patterns and allowed values can be checked on each record alone, for example with a JSON Schema.
misconceptions: A type check looks at one value in one record
A pattern check looks at one value in one record
An allowed-values check looks at one value in one record
